Role of Supra-Segmental Information in Attribution of Meaning
Alison Moy
DEPARTMENT OF COMMUNICATION SCIENCES & DISORDERS
Viorica Marian
FACULTY CO-AUTHOR, DEPARTMENT OF COMMUNICATION SCIENCES AND DISORDERS, NORTHWESTERN UNIVERSITY

Unlike English, Mandarin is a tonal language, meaning it relies on tone distinctions to tell the difference between different words with the same phonemic pronunciation. The present study examined how knowing Mandarin tones influenced English word recognition in Mandarin-English bilinguals, which would suggest that tonal knowledge carries over from Mandarin into English and influences word perception in a non-tonal language.  For this experiment, homophones were presented in different tones, and the word chosen, along with three reaction times, were recorded.  We found that bilinguals did not appear to identify and choose words differently than monolinguals based on the corresponding tone.  However, we did find an apparent processing difference between bilinguals and monolinguals in our reaction time data, which provides support for an interactive account of bilingual spoken language processing.
Background and Introduction

The number of bilingual people in the world is increasing, and many have suggested that the population of bilinguals and multilinguals outnumbers that of monolinguals.  In just the United States, according to the most recent United States Census, approximately 18% of the population (47 million out of 262.4 million people) speaks a language other than English at home.  Among those 47 million, two million speak Mandarin, which is the third most-spoken language in the United States after English and Spanish.¹  In spite of this large population of bilinguals, there is still much more to discover about the complex influence of multiple languages on bilingual language processing.  Previous studies have examined the extent to which multiple languages are processed together or separately and have found that there is parallel activation of lexical items within and between languages.²  However, there has been limited research on the influence of learning a tonal language, such as Mandarin, on perception of a non-tonal language, such as English.

In Mandarin, one of the most important concepts to grasp is that of the four tones—high level, rising, dipping, and falling.  If the wrong tone is used, the meaning changes and a word is likely to be misunderstood.  Therefore, in order to understand Mandarin, one must be trained to distinguish between tones for both production and perception.  It has been suggested that all speakers of Chinese “feel unconsciously that a tone is such an integral part of the word that a syllable of the same consonantal and vocalic makeup but spoken in a different tone sounds like a totally different word.”³  With just a few exceptions, English does not differentiate between tones and stress for meaning (for example, address, as in “a location”, and address, “to speak to”, or produce, the noun, and produce, the verb), so there is usually no confusion regarding word inflection and semantic meaning.  Research on perception of tones has found that tone perception is related to linguistic experience and background; in other words, learning a tonal language influences how well one perceives tones.⁴,⁵  This suggests that Mandarin-English bilinguals may be more likely to recognize and perceive the necessary tones than English monolinguals, who have limited experience with these tones.
